draft.title: Scientific notation
card: A number in scientific notation is written as \(a \times 10^{n}\). Here \(a\) is at least 1 and less than 10, and \(n\) is a whole number.
To write a large number: move the decimal point until the number is from 1 to less than 10. Count the moves. That count is a positive power of 10.
Example: \(52{,}000\) becomes \(5.2\) after 4 moves left, so it is \(5.2 \times 10^{4}\).
For a small number between 0 and 1, the point moves right and the power is negative. For example, \(0.0007 = 7 \times 10^{-4}\). To go back, move the point the other way.
draft.remember: Write a number from 1 to less than 10 times a power of 10. Large numbers have a positive power, small numbers a negative power.

a.why: Moving the point 4 places left gives \(3.6\), so the power is 4. \(36 \times 10^{3}\) has the right value, but 36 is not from 1 to less than 10, so it is not scientific notation.
a.clue: Count how many places the point moves to get 3.6.

b.q: A bacterium in a lab measures \(0.0000045\) m long. Which is this length in scientific notation?
b.why: The point moves 6 places right to give \(4.5\), and the number is less than 1, so the power is \(-6\). The option with \(10^{-5}\) comes from counting one move too few.
b.clue: Count each place the point moves, including the one next to the 4.

problems.detail: The card says n is a 'whole number', but in Australian usage whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, … and exclude negatives. The same card then uses negative powers such as \(10^{-4}\). It should say n is an integer.

check.summary: Both questions and their answers are correct. The card calls the power n a 'whole number', which excludes the negative powers it then uses; it should say 'integer'.

proposal.title: Scientific notation
